title: Throw an error on createVNode with using `innerHTML` and `children` at the same time

judge.reasoning: The issue asks for no error and for the element to show innerHTML when provided, otherwise the children, with both changing dynamically. On the base tree the original crash no longer reproduces (the mount test passes on base), so the live defect is the dynamic case: when innerHTML/textContent goes from a value back to nullish while children are unchanged, the element stays empty because the old child vnodes are still considered mounted but their DOM was replaced. Patch B addresses exactly that in patchElement: it broadens the reset condition from truthy to `!= null` (so an empty-string innerHTML also unsets correctly) and, after clearing the element, puts the still-mounted old children's DOM back (text via hostSetElementText, arrays via move) so the subsequent diff operates on real content. Its tests cover text children, array children with component reuse (no remount), empty-string toggles, textContent, and a compiled block with PROPS patch flags, plus SSR nullish cases; the independent toggle tests go from FAIL on base to PASS with B. Patch A does not change runtime behaviour at all; it only adds a dev warning telling users not to combine innerHTML/textContent with children, which runs contrary to the issue's stated expectation and leaves all three independent toggle scenarios failing exactly as on base. Its tests pass only because they assert the new warning text, not any fix. B's approach carries some risk (moving vnodes whose DOM was detached by innerHTML), but it is targeted, commented, and well exercised, including the block-tree path. B is the better fix.

title: suspense.resolve() is called without a pending branch.

judge.reasoning: Both patches identify the same root cause: when the parent Suspense patches its pending branch with the same root type, a nested suspensible Suspense that flips to synchronous content resolves itself during that patch and immediately decrements the parent's deps to 0, calling parentSuspense.resolve() mid-patch. The parent then falls through to its own post-patch deps check and calls resolve() again with pendingBranch already cleared, producing the reported warning. Both patches defer the parent's resolution until the patch completes, and both pass all five independent tests (base fails four of them with the exact warning). The difference is in mechanism and craft. Patch A temporarily increments and decrements suspense.deps around the patch call. This is minimal but overloads the deps counter, which is meant to count registered async dependencies, with a synthetic placeholder; any other code reading deps during the patch (nested boundary creation, devtools, future callers) sees a misleading count, and if patch throws the counter is permanently off by one so the boundary can never resolve. Patch B adds an explicit isPatchingPendingBranch flag on the boundary, initialized in createSuspenseBoundary and checked only in the nested-suspensible resolve path, which is the one path that can fire synchronously during the patch. This matches the existing isFallbackMountPending convention, states intent clearly, and leaves the deps semantics intact. On tests, Patch A's two tests are good (including a follow-up update that verifies activeBranch isn't corrupted), but Patch B adds three scenarios: the basic mid-patch resolve, a later sibling registering a new async dep during the same patch (verifying the parent keeps waiting), and a multi-root branch with a plain element mounted after the nested boundary. Both sets would fail before the fix. Scope is equivalent and tightly focused in both. Patch B wins on clarity of intent, consistency with surrounding conventions, and marginally broader test coverage, while A's deps hack is terse but less principled.

title: the div which has the ref attribute inside the v-for, when I v-if toggle them, the ref value.length increase more and more

judge.reasoning:
Root cause (both identify it correctly): buildProps skips NEED_PATCH when the element is forced into a block by a dynamic :key, and transformFor then demotes that block to a plain vnode for a stable (constant-source) fragment, leaving a ref/directive/vnode-hook-carrying vnode with no patch flag. The parent block never tracks it, so unmount never calls setRef(null) and the ref array grows. Both patches make the demoted vnode carry NEED_PATCH, and all four independent tests pass on both.

Patch B simply drops the `!shouldUseBlock` guard. That is minimal and runtime-safe (NEED_PATCH on an already-tracked block is redundant and changes no patching path), but it is also incomplete relative to the issue text. The issue explicitly says a function ref 'don't get null'. In the reporter's script-setup environment a `:ref="fn"` binding is SETUP_CONST, so analyzePatchFlag returns early (constant value) before `hasRef = true` is ever set. B leaves that path untouched, so a setup-const function ref in the v-for still gets no NEED_PATCH and is never nulled; the independent function-ref test only passed on B because it was compiled without const binding metadata. B also leaves the before-update ordering broken: a demoted vnode with NEED_PATCH gets tracked after its own dynamic children in the parent block, so a `@vue:before-update` / directive beforeUpdate element with children inside a stable v-for fires after its children update, which is exactly what the forced-block rule exists to prevent. B's snapshot churn (NEED_PATCH added to every forced block with a directive/ref) is harmless but is noise rather than a fix.

Patch A addresses the demotion precisely: buildProps reports `needsPatch` and `isBlockRequired`, transformElement re-validates `needsPatch` against the final patchFlag (so TEXT-flagged nodes don't get a spurious NEED_PATCH, covered by a test), and transformFor ORs in NEED_PATCH only when it actually demotes a block, while keeping the block when a before-update hook with children requires it. It also moves `hasRef = true` ahead of the constant-value early return, so setup-const function refs are tracked, directly covering the issue's function-ref complaint with a dedicated integration test. The camelized `vue:beforeUpdate` match is an adjacent change but small, tested, and consistent with how transformOn normalizes the name.

Tests: both add compiler and compiler+runtime tests that fail on base. A's suite is broader and covers the const function ref, directive unmounted, vnode unmounted, and both beforeUpdate ordering cases; B covers static ref and directive unmount including repeated toggles.

Scope and craft: A is more invasive (two new optional VNodeCall fields) but the extra work is all the same mechanism and resolves parts of the issue B leaves broken. B is cleaner to read but emits a redundant flag on all forced blocks. A wins on correctness against the issue as stated.

title: defineProps options object loses properties when using generics

judge.reasoning:
Both patches restore the missing optional keys, but only Patch A makes the resulting prop types usable. Patch A removes the conditional in `PropMethod` so `PropType<T>` is no longer a deferred type when `T` is a type parameter; this addresses the root cause (the deferral cascading into `RequiredKeys`/`OptionalKeys`) and also lets `InferPropType` resolve to `T`. The added `InferPropType` tweak (`unknown extends D ? V : D`) keeps the inferred value assignable to `V` when no default is present. The independent tests confirm it: all six pass, including the two that check `props.a` is `T | undefined` and `props.c` is `T`, and Patch A's own dts test asserts exact types (`T | null`, `T`, `T | undefined`) plus assignability of `props` to `{ bar: T }`. The `PropMethod` widening is low risk because the new member is structurally a subtype of the existing `{ (): T }` member, so unions and inference are unaffected for non-generic usage.

Patch B wraps the key-check conditionals in `{ p: T[K] }` so the key sets resolve, which fixes the symptom of dropped keys, but leaves the value type as an unresolved `InferPropType<PropType<T>, true>`. The independent tests show this directly: two tests fail on B because `InferPropType<PropType<T>, true> | undefined` is not assignable to `T | undefined`, meaning a generic component still cannot pass `props.a` where `T` is expected. That falls short of the issue's ask that 'the props be declared correctly'. Patch B's own tests only check key existence and `undefined` assignability, never that the types resolve to `T`, so they would not have caught this gap. B also touches more surface (`DefaultKeys`, `PublicRequiredKeys`) without closing the underlying deferral. Patch A is the more correct fix with stronger tests.

title: Clearing `select`'s value in change handler behaviour changed since 3.4.15 via webdriver

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause the same way: instead of blindly skipping `setSelected` while `_assigning` is set, `updated` now compares the model value against what the change listener assigned and re-syncs the DOM when they differ. Both pass all six independent tests, including the single-select-cleared-to-null case from the issue, the fixed-value reset, and the multiple-select reset/in-place mutation cases.

Patch A is the more robust implementation. It compares with `looseEqual`/Set membership, which is the same equality `setSelected` itself uses, so a handler that replaces the model with an equal-but-new array still takes the fast path; Patch B uses `toRaw` identity, which forces a full option rewrite in that case, undermining the perf optimization the original commit introduced. A also clears the pending marker as soon as `updated` consumes it (so any further update in the same tick always syncs), detects `el.multiple` flipping during the pending update, snapshots the Array it hands to user code, and uses try/finally so a throwing assigner cannot leave stale state. B's snapshot/`_assigning` combination is correct for the scenarios in the issue but keeps three parallel fields and leaves `_assigning` semantics overloaded.

On tests, A adds a broader suite (single clear, Set override, duplicate values, multiple→single, Array/Set mutation in handler, no-rewrite guards, assigner throw), all of which exercise real behaviour rather than tautologies. B's five tests are well targeted at the issue (including the 0/1 values from the report) and include a no-re-sync regression guard, but cover fewer edges.

On craft, B is simpler and closer to the surrounding code, and its comment is clearer; A's tuple with `pending[0]`/`pending[1]` indexing is less readable. That readability cost is real but smaller than A's correctness and consistency advantages, so A wins by a moderate margin.

### Vue version

3.4.21

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://play.vuejs.org/#

### Steps to reproduce

👋 sorry I can only reproduce this myself when acting on chrome with webdriver, but I have narrowed it down a lot

the basic premise is we have a strange select that clears its value on change, exampled in the repo link

The bug occurs when _webdriver_ clicks the `select` and clicks one of the `option`s within the value does not get cleared afterwards. If I click in the page myself it clears properly.

### What is expected?

The value of the select afterwards should be null

### What is actually happening?

it is whatever was selected last, ie 0 or 1

### System Info

```shell
System:
    OS: Linux 5.15 Ubuntu 20.04.6 LTS (Focal Fossa)
    CPU: (32) x64 AMD Ryzen 9 5950X 16-Core Processor
    Memory: 55.80 GB / 88.39 GB
    Container: Yes
    Shell: 5.0.17 - /bin/bash
  Binaries:
    Node: 18.16.1 - ~/.nvm/versions/node/v18.16.1/bin/node
    npm: 9.5.1 - ~/.nvm/versions/node/v18.16.1/bin/npm
  Browsers:
    Chrome: 122.0.6261.94
```


### Any additional comments?

I have bisected the releases and found that this first happens from [3.4.15](https://github.com/vuejs/core/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md#3415-2024-01-18). I suspect the change is related to the `select` performance improvement https://github.com/vuejs/core/commit/2ffb956efe692da059f4895669084c5278871351

further i notice the commit introduces and _assigning field which changes the behaviour until the next tick. and wrapping the clearing call in `nextTick` works as a workaround in my instance.

``` js
  nextTick(() => { selection.value = null })
```

I suspect the issue relates to the fact that webdriver submits selection events in a slightly unusual manner. However I think that shouldn't mean this broke but it has

title: Transition should sniff for teleport in custom components

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the root cause the same way: make a Teleport root transparent so transition hooks land on the teleported element, and both pass all six independent tests. The differences are robustness and generality. Patch B adds a dedicated TELEPORT branch to setTransitionHooks, so any Teleport vnode reached through component propagation (including nested components and re-render updates) gets unwrapped, and it guards with isVNode because raw render-function children (e.g. `[cond ? h('div') : null]`) are not normalized at renderComponentRoot time. Patch A instead special-cases only the component subTree path and reuses getInnerChild/findNonCommentChild, which dereferences `c.type` on each child and will throw a TypeError on a null child; A's test only covers the empty-array case, not the null case that B explicitly tests. B's warning helper also correctly treats an empty or single-element Teleport as transitionable and surfaces the existing multi-child warning. On tests, B's unit suite is considerably more thorough (toggle on/off with hook/element assertions, out-in mode, KeepAlive, null children, multi-root warning, and asserts no spurious warning), whereas A's unit tests are thinner (its KeepAlive test exercises existing behavior unrelated to the change), though A does add a useful e2e DOM test. Scope is comparable. Overall B is the more correct and better-tested fix.

title: defineCustomElement can accidentally override members of the Element prototype

judge.reasoning: Both patches satisfy the independent tests, and both add a dev warning when a declared prop collides with an inherited Element member. The difference is what happens after the warning. Patch B still defines the prop on the element and overwrites `tagName` (its own test asserts `e.tagName` becomes 'foo'), so in production builds nothing changes at all and the breakage the issue describes (a `tag-name` attribute clobbering `Element.prototype.tagName`) persists. Patch A addresses the root cause: it walks the prototype chain, refuses to shadow read-only accessors/non-writable values/methods, keeps the attribute-to-prop path working, and adds a `patchProp` branch so a Vue parent can still pass such props (via `_setProp`) without touching the native member. It also hardens the `expose` path with the same check while still permitting intentional method overrides. Its tests are substantive: they assert native `tagName`/`remove` survive, `hasOwnProperty` is false, attribute and parent-driven updates still flow to the prop, and writable reflected members like `title` keep the old mapping. Patch A is larger and has minor craft issues (a `@ts-expect-error` to reach a private field, a `_isVueCE`/`_isProtectedProp` coupling from `patchProp`), and Patch B's one-line `key in proto` check is admittedly simpler and lower risk. But B's test that overrides `hasAttribute` with an object illustrates the hazard of leaving the overwrite in place rather than resolving it. Patch B also includes an unrelated assertion tweak at line 237. Weighing correctness first, A resolves the issue while B only reports it, so A wins.

### Vue version

3.4.5

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://stackblitz.com/edit/vitejs-vite-aob5zf?file=index.html

### Steps to reproduce

I defined a Vue component with `tagName` as a property, and used that, together with `defineCustomElement` to define the `hello-world` webcomponent. 

[`tagName`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/tagName) is obviously already defined in the `Element` prototype.

### What is expected?

I expected to maybe be able to create _only_ the `tag-name` attribute (and no matching `tagName` property), or a warning that I'm accidentally overwriting important `Element` properties. Or a way to remap the `tag-name` attribute to a different property.

### What is actually happening?

Vue's `defineCustomElement` happily overwrites the `tagName` property of the `Element` prototype without warning.

I know this is user error, but I was surprised that Vue let me.

### System Info

_No response_

### Any additional comments?

In Lit, you can be explicit about what property/attribute something maps to, that would be super cool here too:

```ts
@property({ attribute: 'tag-name' }) nonConfictingPropertyName;
```

We managed to put us in a situation where the attribute (which is not problematic) is causing issues because Vue generated an override for the `tagName` property (which is problematic), while we don't use that often.

title: Custom directive's unmounted event is not triggered on v-for element

judge.reasoning:
Both patches identify the same root cause: transformElement skips NEED_PATCH for elements it compiles as blocks (keyed elements, elements with runtime directives/vnode hooks plus children), and transformFor then demotes those blocks to plain vnodes inside a stable fragment without restoring the flag, so the vnode is never in the parent block's dynamicChildren and optimized unmount never runs the directive's unmounted hook. Both add NEED_PATCH back at demotion time, and both pass all five independent reproduction tests. Patch A does this with a new `needsPatchWithoutBlock` helper that re-inspects the VNodeCall's props/directives from inside vFor. It is small and localized, but it duplicates buildProps's own analysis (hasRef/hasVnodeHook/runtimeDirectives) in a second place that can drift, and it unconditionally demotes the block. That discards a guarantee buildProps deliberately encodes: elements with a runtime directive or vue:before-update hook plus children are forced into blocks specifically so beforeUpdate runs before children patch. Under A, `
{{x}}
` becomes a non-block vnode whose children are tracked ahead of it in dynamicChildren, so hooks now fire but in the wrong order. Patch B threads the decision data out of buildProps (`needsPatch`, `isBlockRequired`) onto the VNodeCall, so vFor uses the same analysis the element transform used rather than re-deriving it. It only demotes when the block was not required for ordering, and keeps the block (which is still tracked by the parent block) when a before-update hook or directive with children needs it. It also correctly recomputes needsPatch after transformElement may have added TEXT, and tests that case. The hasRef reorder (so setup-const function refs are tracked) and the camelized `vue:beforeUpdate` match are adjacent fixes outside the issue's ask, but they are coherent with the same root cause, are covered by tests, and don't add meaningful risk. B is more invasive (ast.ts field additions, buildProps return shape), which costs it some scope/craft points, and the shadowed `needsPatch` plus `as PatchFlags` cast are slightly awkward. Tests: both add compiler-level assertions and runtime integration tests that fail on base. B's tests additionally cover the ordering and non-NEED_PATCH cases that distinguish the approaches. On balance B resolves the issue more correctly: it restores tracking without breaking the before-update ordering invariant the compiler already relies on, and it uses a single source of truth for the decision. A is a reasonable minimal fix but leaves a semantic regression path in the demoted-block case.

title: Vue is not catching errors on server side in SSR when using async child setup

judge.reasoning: Patch A addresses the root cause: when a component's async setup rejects during SSR, the rejection is re-thrown from the SSR-only catch in setupStatefulComponent (after handleError has already notified errorCaptured/errorHandler), and renderComponentVNode now detects that rejection and emits a `<!---->` placeholder instead of calling renderComponentSubTree with a half-initialized instance. That matches the issue's ask: errorCaptured fires once, the child template is never rendered with missing state, and siblings still render. The rethrow is confined to the isSSR branch and is caught by the renderer's own chain, so the client path is unaffected. Its tests cover await-then-throw, compiled ssrRender, and app.config.errorHandler, and it updates existing expectations that previously encoded the buggy behaviour (rendering children / 'missing template' warnings after a rejected setup). Patch B only wraps the sync render path in try/catch and routes render errors through handleError; it still renders the failed child's template, so the parent receives a second spurious TypeError and props-only templates still emit markup. Its own test enshrines that double-error behaviour, which is the symptom the issue complains about. The independent tests confirm: A passes all four, B fails the three that check the template is not rendered and that only the setup error is captured.

issue_md:
### Vue version

3.5.13

### Link to minimal reproduction

[Vue SFC Playground](https://play.vuejs.org/#__SSR__)

### Steps to reproduce

Just open a link and you will see errors when SSR is ON.
When SSR is OFF everything works as expected.

Also, commeting the line with top-level await (making `Comp.vue` a sync component) will also work fine both with and without SSR.

### What is expected?

In SSR mode the page is expected to be blank white for 1 second and then display error message from `App.vue`.
This works as expected with SSR turned off.

Basically `onErrorCaptured` should be triggered, child setup and `<template>` render immediately stopped and error message from parent component shown.

### What is actually happening?

In SSR mode the page is blank for 1 second but then it tries to render the `<template>` of `Comp.vue` using the data that might not even exist (because it appears in `setup` after throwing error).

And even if it manages to render `<template>` correctly, it still does not trigger `onErrorCaptured` in `App.vue` and do not switch to show error message.

### Any additional comments?

I am building a custom rendering package built on top of Vue and it heavily uses structures like these:

```vue
 // Wrappers are supposed to catch ALL errors and throws in child <Block /> and show nice error message

<BlockWrapper>
    <Block ... />
</BlockWrapper>

<BlockWrapper>
    <Block ... />
</BlockWrapper>

<BlockWrapper>
    <Block ... />
</BlockWrapper>

...
```

Because of this bug OR my misunderstanding of how to handle async errors in Vue 3, even when thrown it still tries to render child block's `<template>` even with missing data (because setup is stopped executing), throws on reading properties of non-existing objects and the whole Nuxt page breaks.

Please, don't tell me this is a no-fix. It would be a disaster... 😭

title: $el of templateRef points to comment VNode instead of first real child of component

judge.reasoning: Both patches share the same core approach: when the component's subTree is a DEV_ROOT_FRAGMENT, use filterSingleRoot to find the lone real root and expose its el as $el, and both follow HOC chains. The decisive difference is that Patch A gates the entire fix behind `__DEV__`, so a template compiled with comments preserved (DEV_ROOT_FRAGMENT set) but running on a production runtime still gets the comment node as `$el`. That is precisely the reporter's setup: the linked reproduction is in the playground's `__PROD__` mode, which pairs a dev-built compiler-sfc with the prod runtime. Patch B explicitly notes this case in its doc comment and resolves it unconditionally, so it fixes the issue as reported; Patch A would leave the reporter's own repro broken. Patch B's resolution also degrades safely: if the inner component has no subTree yet or no dev fragment, `getSingleRootEl` falls through to the existing `vnode.el`. On tests, Patch B adds a compiler-integration test in packages/vue that mirrors the issue (real `<!-- comment --><div>` template, click listener via $el, and v-if swap of the ref target), plus runtime-test unit cases for nested fragments, HOC chains with re-render, and a guard that true multi-root components keep the fragment anchor. Patch A's tests are hand-built block vnodes and include useful Suspense and mounting-safety cases, and its Suspense traversal is a genuine extra that B lacks, but that is adjacent to the ask. Scope and craft are comparable; A's `found` flag and B's mutual recursion are both readable. The `__DEV__` gating is a correctness gap on the reported scenario, so B wins.

### Vue version

3.5.15

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://play.vuejs.org/#__PROD__

### Steps to reproduce

Hi, I just spent some hours debugging a very strange behavior when accessing the underlying element of a component ref by using `templateRef.$el`. The component I placed the template ref on had only one root level `<div>` inside its template, however there was a comment above it. It looks like this leads to the element being referenced by the template ref being the VNode of this comment instead of the `<div>` element.

Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the [Playground](https://play.vuejs.org/#__PROD__)
2. Open the console and see that the element referenced by `childRef.value.$el` is a text VNode
3. Click on the text "Test" in the preview (Nothing should be logged to the console)
4. Go into the component "Child.vue" and remove the comment in line 2
5. After a hot reload (or manual one) `childRef.value.$el` should point to the div element as logged to the console. Clicking on the text "Test" in the preview should now also log "Clicked Test" to the console

### What is expected?

I would expect `templateRef.$el` to point to the first real element inside the component excluding comments.

### What is actually happening?

`templateRef.$el` points to a VNode for the comment inside the components template.

### System Info

_No response_

_No response_

title: Preserve input values entered during hydration

judge.reasoning: Both patches use the same detection idea (directive `created` running on an element that already has a parentNode means hydration) and both defer the decision to `mounted`, which correctly covers the Suspense/async-deps case. The difference is coverage. Patch B only preserves input when `el.type` is exactly 'text' or 'textarea', so a v-model on type=email, password, number, search, url or tel is still reset after hydration, and checkboxes, radios and selects are untouched. The issue is about inputs and forms generally, and the independent tests confirm B still fails for email, checkbox and select while A passes all of them. B's `mounted` also calls `castValue(el.value, trim, number)` without the `type === 'number'` fallback that `created` uses, so a `<input type=number v-model>` would sync a string instead of a number. Patch A handles vModelText (with a cloned-node probe to distinguish browser sanitization from user input, e.g. color lowercasing and range clamping), vModelCheckbox (including shared array/Set models across several checkboxes synced in the same tick), vModelRadio and vModelSelect (single and multiple, with correct default-selection logic). Its test suite is substantial and targeted: typed text, modifiers, textarea, dynamic type, untouched inputs, boolean and true/false-value checkboxes, multiple checkboxes, radio, select single/multiple, sanitized values, and input during pending async hydration. A is considerably larger and the per-tick `hydrationModelValues` map for shared checkbox models is somewhat intricate, but it is scoped to the hydration path, documented, and exercised by tests. B's single test covers only the narrowest case. On correctness and tests A clearly wins; its extra breadth is in service of the issue rather than unrelated churn.

### Vue version

3.5.27

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/issues/29206

### Steps to reproduce

user loads a page with a slow internet connection
starts entering some values ​​into the input with v-model
after all browser resources loaded - input v-model reset to default value

### What is expected?

entered input value is preserved once hydration completes

### What is actually happening?

input value is reset to its default value

### System Info

```shell

```

### Any additional comments?

This is affecting UX when interacting with inputs/forms in slowly loading apps, where values entered during hydration phase are erased and the progress is lost. I have been blocking all forms myself until mounted hook fires to workaround this issue - it would be great to not have to!

title: v-model on <select multiple> uses stale collection type after switching between Array and Set

judge.reasoning: The source changes are byte-identical: both patches replace the `isSetModel` captured in `created` with an `el._modelValue` field that is initialized in `created` and refreshed in `beforeUpdate`, so the change handler reads the current model type. This correctly fixes the root cause (stale closure capture) and all five independent tests pass identically for A and B. The only difference is the test coverage. Patch A adds one test that starts from an Array, switches to a Set, then back to an Array, checking the emitted type each time. Patch B adds two tests, one starting from Array and one from Set, each performing an interaction before the switch (matching the issue's 'interact with the select again' scenario), verifying that setSelected reflects the new model after the switch, and then switching back. B's tests more faithfully cover both directions described in the issue (steps 2-4 and step 5) and exercise the case where the handler had already run with the old type. Both test sets would fail before and pass after the fix. Scope and craft are equal otherwise, so B wins on test thoroughness by a modest margin.

### Vue version

3.5.39

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://play.vuejs.org/#__PROD__

### Steps to reproduce

1. Bind a `<select multiple v-model>` to an Array.
2. Switch the bound value to a Set at runtime.
3. Interact with the select again.
4. The emitted model becomes an Array again.
5. Switching back from Set -> Array shows the same stale-type behavior in reverse.

### What is expected?

The current collection type should be respected after the model switches at runtime.


### What is actually happening?

The change handler keeps using the collection type captured when the directive was created, so the first user interaction after a runtime Array/Set switch emits the old type.

title: Scoped slot transforms array argument if rendered conditionally

judge.reasoning:
Both patches take the same core approach: stop merging the compiler-generated branch key into a single `v-bind` expression on a slot outlet and instead pass the key as a separate sixth `renderSlot()` argument, with `props.key || key` priority at runtime. The independent tests pass on both. The differences are at the edges.

Patch A is more correct. (1) It adds `if (props == null) props = {}` in `renderSlot`. This matters: before either patch, `<slot v-if="ok" v-bind="maybeNull" />` worked because `mergeProps({key:0}, null)` yields an object; after Patch B, the slot now receives `normalizeProps(guardReactiveProps(null))` = `null` and `props.key` (and `Object.keys(props)` in custom-element mode) throws. Patch B therefore regresses a previously working case; Patch A covers it and tests it. (2) Patch A fixes `guardReactiveProps` to `slice()` arrays instead of `extend({}, arr)`, so a reactive array (e.g. an auto-unwrapped `ref([])`) bound to the slot stays an array. Without this, Patch B still turns reactive arrays into index-keyed objects, which is exactly the symptom the issue reports, just via a different code path. (3) Patch A suppresses the `ref_for` marker merge for slot outlets inside `v-for`, so `<slot v-for ... v-bind="arr">` no longer gets `mergeProps({ref_for:true}, arr)`; this is the v-for counterpart of the same array-to-object conversion and is tested.

Scope and craft: Patch A's compiler change is narrow, adding one branch in `injectProp` only for the single-expression case and leaving existing object-props codegen and snapshots untouched. Patch B reroutes all slot key injection through the new argument, requiring snapshot churn, and includes a misplaced snapshot entry (a `compiler: v-for` snapshot added to `transformElement.spec.ts.snap`, apparently duplicated), which is sloppy. Patch B's unit tests for `renderSlot` are reasonable, but Patch A also adds end-to-end compiler+runtime tests covering v-if, v-else, template v-if, template v-for, v-for, objects, nullish, reactive arrays, custom-element mode, and branch toggling.

Patch B's uniform 'key is always a separate arg' design is cleaner conceptually, but the nullish regression and the unhandled reactive-array case outweigh that. Patch A is the better fix.

issue_md: ### Vue version 3.5.0 ### Link to minimal reproduction https://play.vuejs.org/# ### Steps to reproduce 1. Create a component with a scoped slot that is rendered conditionally 2. Pass an array as the sole argument to the slot ### What is expected? Array is rendered normally. If you render items of that array in `v-for` loop, you only see items inside that array ### What is actually happening? Array is transformed into object. Items and their indexes are staying the same, `key` field is added ### System Info ```shell ``` ### Any additional comments? `key` attribute is generated by the compiler for the slot rendered with `v-if`. While this is not explicitly mentioned in documentation, one can assume that the expectation is that `slotProps` is always an object, as this is what will be passed to the slot if you use multiple `v-bind` directives on the slot. This issue is rather pointing out the difference in behavior of the slot when `v-if` is present or not present.

title: SSR memory leak after a render error in a dynamic component

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the reported leak and pass all four independent tests, so the decision rests on robustness and completeness. The root cause is that a throw inside the vdom fallback path (renderSlot/withCtx under a dynamic component) leaves `blockStack`/`currentBlock` populated, so every later `createVNode` is pushed into a stale, module-level block array and retained forever.

Patch A adds a `resetBlocks()` helper that clears both `blockStack` and `currentBlock`, and calls it at the two component render boundaries: `renderComponentRoot` (client/render-function path) and the SSR `renderComponentSubTree` ssrRender path. This follows the pre-existing design in `renderComponentRoot`, which already reset `blockStack.length = 0` on error, and it fixes that reset's latent incompleteness (it never cleared `currentBlock`, so vnodes created afterwards still went into the stale block until the next `closeBlock`). Because it resets at the boundary, it is a catch-all for any helper that opens a block and throws, not just the two helpers identified. In SSR no blocks are legitimately open when a component subtree renders (render functions run to completion before the buffer is walked), so a full reset is safe. Tests are thorough: a runtime-core unit test checking `blockStack`/`currentBlock` after a throwing render, an SSR test reproducing the issue and asserting block state directly, and a GC test wired into the `--expose-gc` project.

Patch B unwinds blocks locally in `renderSlot` (with a try/catch plus moving `_d = true` into a finally, which is good craft) and in `withCtx`. This is precise and preserves outer blocks, and its v-if test is a nice addition. However, it only covers the two openers it identified; any other block-opening path that throws during SSR vdom fallback would still leak, and it leaves the incomplete `blockStack.length = 0` reset in `renderComponentRoot` untouched, so `currentBlock` can still be stale there on the client. Its test coverage is a single GC file with no direct assertion on block state.

A addresses the problem at the boundary where errors are already handled, fixes the pre-existing partial reset, and ships more diagnostic tests, so it is the more complete and robust fix. B is a reasonable, targeted alternative but narrower.

- run `pnpm i && pnpm leak`
- see the heap size & alive app instances grow with each request after the single failed render

The script renders 500 fresh SSR apps, which all get garbage-collected. Then renders **one** app whose slot content throws, then renders 500 more identical healthy apps, which will never be garbage collected afterwards.

A dynamic component `<component :is>` with a `<slot />` is needed for this to reproduce.

Card

```vue
<script setup>
    defineProps({ tag: { type: String, default: 'div' } })
</script>

<template>
    <component :is="tag" class="card">
        <slot />
    </component>
</template>
```

app:

```vue
<script setup>
    defineProps(['payload'])  // one request renders with `payload: null` → throws
</script>

<template>
    <main>
        <Card>{{ payload.title }}</Card>
    </main>
</template>
```

### What is expected?

A failed `renderToString` should not affect subsequent renders and all apps rendered after it should get garbage collected.

Every app created after the single failed render is kept in memory forever.

```
--- phase 2: 500 healthy renders (identical to phase 1) ---
after 500: created=1001 finalized=500 alive=501 heap=29.0MB
```

title: SSR hydration warning: dynamic props on SVG elements are patched as properties instead of attributes

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the root cause identically: they derive the element's namespace from `el.namespaceURI` and pass it to `patchProp` in the dynamic-props hydration branch, so runtime-dom's `shouldSetAsProp` routes SVG/MathML props to `setAttribute`. The independent tests confirm both resolve every scenario. The differences are in tests and craft. Patch A's tests emulate the browser's read-only IDL getters (viewBox, r, foreignObject width) and assert that no 'Failed setting prop' warning and no mismatch warning is emitted while the attribute value is preserved; this directly mirrors the issue's symptom and would fail on base. Patch B sets `__DEV__ = false` in both tests, which suppresses the very warning the issue is about and makes the tests rely on attribute values instead; its first test also does not define a read-only property, so on jsdom (where `width`/`viewBox` are not on the element) the key-in-el check already falls through to setAttribute and the test likely passes on base, making it weak evidence. Only B's second test (with the defined getter) reliably fails before the fix. On craft, A factors the namespace detection into a small documented helper that distinguishes element namespace from `getContainerType`'s foreignObject handling, and avoids B's non-null assertions on `namespaceURI`. A's additional use of the helper in the `onClick` branch is harmless (events ignore namespace) and neutral. Overall A is the better-tested, cleaner fix.

### Steps to reproduce
1. Open the reproduction.
2. Open the browser devtools **Console**.
3. Observe the `[Vue warn]: Failed setting prop …` error logged during hydration.

### What is expected?
During hydration, dynamic props on SVG (and MathML) elements `width`, `height`, `viewBox`, etc.  should be patched as **attributes** (via `setAttribute`) exactly as they are during normal client-side rendering. Hydration should be silent.

### What is actually happening?
Since 3.5.39, dynamic props on SVG elements are patched as **DOM properties** during hydration, which throws for read-only SVG IDL properties:

```
    at patchDOMProp
    at patchProp
    at hydrateElement
    at hydrateNode
    at hydrateSubTree
    at <App>
```

Nothing is visually broken but the console is flooded with warnings.

title: EffectScope stop() causes runtime crash (Cannot read properties of undefined) when dynamic scope cleanup mutates parent.scopes array during traversal

judge.reasoning: Both patches apply the same root-cause fix: snapshot this.scopes (and this.effects in resume) before iterating in pause()/resume()/stop(), so a child's cleanup or a resumed sync watcher that stops a sibling cannot shift indices under the cached-length loop. All four independent tests pass on both, so correctness is equivalent for the reported scenarios. The only source difference is that Patch A also copies this.effects in pause(); effect.pause() runs no user callbacks, so this is unneeded but harmless, and A's comments explain why each copy exists, which is a small craft plus. The real separation is in tests. Patch A adds three tests: parent stop where a child disposes a sibling (asserting parent and all children inactive and every dispose spy called exactly once), parent resume where a child's sync watcher stops a sibling scope while asserting the other siblings resume and still fire, and resume where a watcher stops a sibling watcher. Patch B adds two: the stop case (only asserting no throw and the sibling inactive) and the sibling-watcher resume case; it does not exercise the resume() path over this.scopes, which the issue explicitly names as affected and which the independent harness tested. A's tests cover more of the issue's stated surface with stronger assertions. Neither patch has unrelated churn. A wins narrowly on test coverage and clarity.

### Vue version

3.5.28

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://play.vuejs.org/#

### Steps to reproduce

Open the reproduction link.
Click the "Trigger сrash" button.
Observe the output status on the screen or check the browser console.

### What is expected?

The parent scope should stop all its children successfully. When a child scope stops a sibling scope during the cleanup phase, the parent traversal loop should handle the array mutation gracefully without throwing errors.

### What is actually happening?

The application crashes with the following error: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'stop')

This happens because EffectScope.stop loops over this.scopes using a cached length l. During iteration, one child's onScopeDispose calls stop() on its sibling. The sibling removes itself from the parent's scopes array, reducing the array size. When the parent loop continues to the cached index l, it tries to access an element out of bounds (which is undefined), causing the runtime crash.

### System Info

```shell
System: OS: macOS, Browser: Chrome, Node: v20.19.5
```

### Any additional comments?

The bug lies in packages/reactivity/src/effectScope.ts.

Inside EffectScope, the methods pause(), resume(), and stop() loop over this.scopes using a cached length without accounting for array mutations. Creating a shallow copy of the array before iterating (e.g. const scopes = this.scopes.slice()) safely resolves the issue.

title: hydrateOnVisible: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'nodeType') when the SSR node is detached before the IntersectionObserver callback fires

judge.reasoning: Both patches stop the reported crash at the real trigger: the async wrapper's performHydrate now bails when the SSR node has no parent, so getContainerType(parentNode(node)) is never reached with null. Both pass the two independent tests that reproduce the issue's actual scenarios (node removed from its parent; app unmounted while the observer callback is queued). The one divergence is the third independent test: when only an ancestor is detached, B skips hydration and A hydrates the still-parented subtree. That matches the issue's 'should not be hydrated' wording, but it is not the crash, and A's choice is deliberate and defensible: A ships a test showing that a subtree temporarily detached (e.g. moved into KeepAlive's storage container) and re-attached still becomes interactive. Under B, that scenario is a regression: hydrateOnVisible calls ob.disconnect() before hydrate(), and hydrateOnIdle has no retry, so a component whose subtree happened to be detached when the trigger fired is skipped permanently and never hydrates after re-attachment. B's wasConnected heuristic only protects the never-connected (test container) case, not temporary detachment. A also adds the defense-in-depth the issue asked for (getContainerType tolerates null, the non-null assertion at the call site is removed), guards instance.isUnmounted explicitly, and brings a much broader test suite: strategy skip, unmount, re-attach, still-attached, a real hydrateOnVisible mock, and the no-strategy path asserting no unhandledRejection. B's tests are adequate but narrower. On correctness A is safer (never throws, never strands a component), on tests A is stronger, and its extra scope is low-risk and issue-requested.

issue_md:
### Vue version

3.5.33 

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://stackblitz.com/edit/vitejs-vite-ktsycrrc?file=repro.mjs

### Steps to reproduce

1. SSR-render an async component that uses hydrate: hydrateOnVisible().
2. On the client, hydration is deferred and the strategy registers an IntersectionObserver on the component's SSR node.
3. The node gets detached from the document before the observer's callback executes (in production this is a route change / re-render while the intersection callback is already queued).
4. The observer callback runs and invokes hydrate() against the now-detached node.

### What is expected?

A node that is no longer connected to the document should simply not be hydrated (there's nothing to hydrate), no exception thrown.

### What is actually happening?

hydrate() reaches hydrateNode, which computes the container type from the node's parent:

```
// packages/runtime-core/src/hydration.ts — inside hydrateNode, async-component branch
nextNode = vnode.type.hydrate(
  node, vnode, parentComponent, parentSuspense,
  getContainerType(parentNode(node)),   // parentNode(node) === null for a detached node
  slotScopeIds, optimized, rendererInternals, hydrateNode,
)
```

```
// packages/runtime-core/src/hydration.ts
const getContainerType = (container) => {
  if (container.nodeType !== 1) return undefined   // <-- container is null -> throws
  ...
}
```

For a detached node parentNode(node) is null, so getContainerType(null) throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'nodeType').

The async-component hydration wrapper only guards against the patched case, never against disconnection:

```
// packages/runtime-core/src/apiAsyncComponent.ts — __asyncHydrate
const performHydrate = () => {
  if (patched) { /* warn + */ return }   // only guards `patched`
  hydrate()                              // no isConnected check
}
```
Because the strategy runs inside load().then(...), the throw surfaces as an unhandledrejection, so app-level try/catch around the component can't catch it.

### System Info

```shell
vue: 3.5.33
@vue/server-renderer: 3.5.33
Environment where it triggers: Android WebView (Chrome), production SSR + client hydration
```

### Any additional comments?

We see this almost exclusively on Android Chrome WebView (~43k occurrences / ~12.8k users over a rollout window) on a page that lazy-hydrates several below-the-fold sections via hydrateOnVisible. The IntersectionObserver callback is dispatched asynchronously; when the user navigates/re-renders in the WebView, the observed node is detached between the intersection being recorded and the callback running, exactly the sequence above. Desktop rarely hits the race.

Skip hydration when the anchor node is no longer connected. the semantically correct place is the async performHydrate (or each built-in strategy's trigger), e.g. bail when no observed/anchor element isConnected:
 
```
const performHydrate = () => {
  if (patched) { return }
  if (el && !el.isConnected) return   // detached before hydration → nothing to hydrate
  hydrate()
}
```
As defense-in-depth, getContainerType could also tolerate a `null` container `(if (!container || container.nodeType !== 1) return undefined)`, since it's called with parentNode(node) at several sites.

We're currently shipping a userland wrapper around hydrateOnVisible that applies exactly the isConnected guard, which fully stops the crash.

title: defineModel: named model with PropType + factory default infers wrong generic (regression from #14968)

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make the same core change: they reorder the overload intersection so `DefineModelRuntimeOptions<T, G, S>` (which carries `type: PropType<T>`) precedes the `{ default } | { required }` union, so TS collects the `PropType<T>` candidate before the candidate derived from the factory default. The independent tests confirm both patches turn the three base failures into passes, so neither leaves the reported scenario broken.

The difference is in how deeply each addresses the root cause the issue names: 'TS infers the generic T from the default factory function's own type (() => never[])'. That candidate comes from the `T extends NativeType ? T : never` branch of `InferDefault`, which lets TS propose the whole function as T. Patch B only changes candidate ordering, so the bogus function-as-T candidate still exists and simply loses to the `PropType` candidate when one is present. Patch A also rewrites `DefineModelDefault<T>` as `(T | ((props: Data) => T)) & NoInfer<InferDefault<Data, T>>`: the naked-union form is the standard TS idiom for inferring T from a factory's return, the factory member matches first so T is never inferred as the function itself, and `NoInfer` keeps `InferDefault` purely as a validator (raw array/object defaults still must use a factory). That removes the faulty inference site rather than just outranking it, and it also covers the factory-default-without-`type` case (`defineModel('count', { default: () => [1] })`), which A explicitly asserts yields `Ref<number[]>`; B does not test or address that path.

Tests: A adds considerably broader dts coverage: named and unnamed PropType+factory, object PropType, Function-typed models (where the default is not a factory), `type: Number` with factory, `required: true` plus default, the explicit-generic workaround, plus negative cases (named raw-object default, factory/runtime mismatch for both overloads, scalar type/default mismatch). B adds the two positive cases from the issue and one mismatch negative test. Both sets would fail before and pass after for the issue scenario.

Scope and craft: A's extra type change is modest, targeted at the exact mechanism the issue identifies, and documented with a clear comment explaining both the naked-union inference and why overload member order matters. B is smaller and lower-risk but relies solely on candidate ordering. On balance A is the more complete, better-tested fix.

### Vue version

3.5.39

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://play.vuejs.org/#

### Steps to reproduce

In the reproduction, `broken` declares a named model with a runtime `type: PropType<string[]>` plus a factory `default: () => []`. `fixed` declares the same thing but with the generic pinned explicitly (`defineModel<string[]>(...)`).

Run the type checker (or `vue-tsc --noEmit` locally) over this SFC.

### What is expected?

Both `broken` and `fixed` should type-check cleanly — this is the recommended pattern for avoiding shared mutable state (per #14966 / #14968): a factory default combined with a runtime `PropType` declaration.


### What is actually happening?

Only `broken` fails. TS infers the generic `T` from the `default` factory function's own type (`() => never[]`) instead of from the `type: PropType<string[]>` field:

error TS2769: No overload matches this call.
Overload 1 of 4, '(name: string, options: ({ required: true; } | { default: DefineModelDefault<() => never[]>; }) & Omit<PropOptions<() => never[], () => never[]>, "default"> & DefineModelOptions<...>): ModelRef<...>', gave the following error.
Type 'PropType<string[]>' is not assignable to type 'true | PropType<() => never[]> | null | undefined'.
Type 'new (...args: any[]) => string[]' is not assignable to type 'true | PropType<() => never[]> | null | undefined'.
Type 'new (...args: any[]) => string[]' is not assignable to type 'new (...args: any[]) => () => never[]'.
Type 'string[]' is not assignable to type '() => never[]'.
Type 'string[]' provides no match for the signature '(): never[]'.
Overload 2 of 4, '(name: string, options?: DefineModelRuntimeOptions<string[], string[], string[]> | undefined): ModelRef<string[] | undefined, string, string[] | undefined, string[] | undefined>', gave the following error.
Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'default' does not exist in type 'DefineModelRuntimeOptions<string[], string[], string[]>'.

his is a regression from #14968 (landed in 3.5.39), which introduced `DefineModelDefault<T> = InferDefault<Data, T>` for the named-model overload. When both a runtime `type: PropType<T>` field and a factory `default` are present on the same options object, TS resolves `T` from the `default` field first, breaking a pattern that worked prior to 3.5.39.

**Workaround:** explicitly pin the generic, as shown by `fixed` in the reproduction:

```ts
const fixed = defineModel<string[]>('visibility2', {
  type: Array as PropType<string[]>,
  default: () => [],
})
```

### System Info

```shell
vue: 3.5.39
vue-tsc: 3.3.7
typescript: 5.7.3
```

### Any additional comments?

Related to / regression from #14966 and #14968. Only reproduces on the **named** `defineModel(name, options)` overload when `type`/`PropType` and a factory `default` are combined; the unnamed `defineModel<T>({ ... })` form with an explicit generic is unaffected.

title: SSR memory leak - options API watchers are created and never stopped with async `setup()`

judge.reasoning: The runtime change is byte-for-byte the same in both patches: wrap the deferred handleSetupResult call in setInSSRSetupState(true)/finally setInSSRSetupState(false), so applyOptions runs with isInSSRComponentSetup set and the options-API watch/computed paths take the SSR branch (non-immediate, non-sync watchers become no-ops; sync ones register with ctx.__watcherHandles). This is the right root-cause fix in both, and all five independent tests go from FAIL on base to PASS on both. The differences are in craft and tests. Patch B adds a comment explaining why the state has to be restored (setupComponent already reset it before the promise resolved), which is exactly the non-obvious thing a future reader needs. Patch B's tests also cover more of the issue's stated expectation ('the same behavior as with a synchronous setup'): the plain repro, an immediate watcher that fires once and never again, and a flush:'sync' watcher that is registered in __watcherHandles and stopped after render. Patch A adds the repro plus a WeakRef/gc leak test; that targets the headline leak directly and matches the existing gc describe block's convention, but it is skipped unless the runner exposes gc, so it rarely executes. Neither adds unrelated churn. B wins on explanatory comment and broader, always-run behavioral coverage; the margin is modest since the fix itself is identical.

title: compileScript drops template imports from __returned__ when analysis re-runs on a transformed template AST

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause the same way: when the shared descriptor's template AST has already been transformed in place by compileTemplate, the import-usage/v-model analysis re-parses the SFC source instead of walking the mutated tree, mirroring the existing guard in compileTemplate. Both pass the five core independent tests (expression, v-for, components/directives, v-model demotion, 600-file cache eviction).

The deciding difference is correctness of the re-parse. Patch B always calls compiler-dom's parse with default options, ignoring any template compiler options. The descriptor's original AST was parsed with the user's templateParseOptions (e.g. custom delimiters, custom compiler, isCustomElement), so B's re-parsed AST can differ from the <500 case, which is precisely the issue's expectation ("same output as when fewer than 500 templates are compiled"). The independent custom-delimiters test confirms this: B still drops the import (FAIL-EXC) while A passes. Patch A threads options.templateOptions (compiler, compilerOptions, ssr) into the analysis and reuses one shared resolveTemplateAST helper for both compileTemplate and the analysis, so the re-parse uses the same configuration compileTemplate itself uses; plugin-vue does pass templateOptions to compileScript, so this holds in the real scenario.

Tests: B's tests are more direct and cover more cases (v-for, v-model, recoverable parse error), while A's test exports the cache to simulate eviction and specifically covers custom delimiters. Both tests fail before and pass after. Scope: A's refactor of compileTemplate into a shared helper is small churn but reduces duplication and keeps the two guards consistent; exporting templateAnalysisCache for tests is a minor wart. Craft is comparable. The remaining correctness gap in B with non-default parser options outweighs its somewhat better test coverage, so A is the better fix.

title: Suspense: flushing buffered effects overflows the call stack when many effects accumulate while pending (RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded)

judge.reasoning: Both patches replace the three spread pushes the issue names (queuePostFlushCb, the nested flushPostFlushCbs merge, and the Suspense merge into a pending parent) with index loops, and both pass the independent tests that reproduce the issue's scenarios. The difference is in completeness and test coverage. Patch A also converts the fourth spread site, `suspense.effects.push(...fn)` in queueEffectWithSuspense, which is the exact path the issue says buffers effects into the suspense; a component with a large hook array would overflow there even with Patch B applied. Patch A's Suspense.spec tests exercise the actual boundary (500k hooks under a pending Suspense, and the nested-parent merge), so they fail on base and would also fail on Patch B at the queueEffectWithSuspense spread, proving the extra site matters. Patch B's tests only cover the scheduler functions directly and never go through Suspense, so they do not guard the merge-into-parent change it makes. Scope and craft are otherwise equivalent: same loop idiom, explanatory comments in both. Patch A is the more complete fix with stronger regression tests.

issue_md:
### Vue version

3.5.39 (also reproduces on 3.5.40 / `@b5f8518` in the playground)

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://play.vuejs.org/#

### Steps to reproduce

1. Open the playground and show the **Preview** pane.
2. The app renders a `<Suspense>` whose default slot contains an async component (resolves after ~4s) plus a large tree (2000 rows, each with a few `flush: 'post'` watchers).
3. While the suspense is pending, a timer keeps mutating a ref, so the still-mounted tree re-renders repeatedly. Each re-render buffers its post effects into `suspense.effects` (via `queueEffectWithSuspense`).
4. When the async component resolves, the suspense flushes the buffered effects.

### What is expected?

The buffered effects flush and the app keeps working.

### What is actually happening?

`Uncaught (in promise): RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` — thrown from `queuePostFlushCb` called by `suspense.resolve()`:

```text
RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
    at queuePostFlushCb (runtime-core.esm-bundler.js:331)
    at Object.resolve   (runtime-core.esm-bundler.js:7426)
```

The scheduler dies mid-flush, leaving the app permanently wedged (blank page).

### Root cause

`suspense.effects` is unbounded — every post effect of every component under a pending suspense boundary is buffered into it. On resolve, the whole array is flushed with a spread call:

- `scheduler.ts`: `pendingPostFlushCbs.push(...cb)`
- `scheduler.ts` (`flushPostFlushCbs` nested case): `activePostFlushCbs.push(...deduped)`
- `Suspense.ts` (merge into pending parent): `parent.effects.push(...effects)`

Spreading an array into a function call is limited by the engine's call stack (~100k–200k args in V8), so once enough effects accumulate the flush itself throws.

### Real-world impact

We hit this in production in a Nuxt app: a kanban board page with ~1000 mounted cards that re-renders once per second (elapsed-time ticker). Navigating to another page keeps the board mounted under `<NuxtPage>`'s pending Suspense; its buffered effects exceed the spread limit and every SPA navigation away from the board crashes with a permanent white screen (hard reload of the target URL works fine, since there is no pending suspense in that case).

### Suggested fix

Replace the unbounded spread pushes with plain loops. I have a PR ready with the fix and a regression test (queuePostFlushCb with a 1M-entry array).

title: Custom elements: async components nested ≥3 levels crash with `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'provides')` — chained child resolve races its parent's mount

judge.reasoning:
Both patches attack the same root cause: the child's chain promise settled when the parent's `_resolveDef()` returned rather than when the parent mounted. Patch A fixes it by making `_resolveDef()` return the async `_pendingResolve` and returning it from the chain callback; Patch B fixes it by returning `this._pendingResolve` from the chain callback after calling `_resolveDef()`. Both make the chain settle after the parent's `resolve()` (which calls `_mount` synchronously), so the independent 3- and 4-level tests pass under either.

B goes further on correctness in a way that is tied to the same crash: it moves the `parent._pendingResolve` check ahead of the `_resolved` check, so an already-resolved child connected under a pending async parent is also deferred instead of mounting immediately into `_inheritParentContext` with `parent._instance === null`. Under A that path still dereferences a null parent instance. A's extra `isConnected` guard is a reasonable hardening against mounting a detached element, but it addresses a pre-existing behavior unrelated to the reported null dereference.

On tests, A's test is more deterministic (controlled promise resolution rather than real setTimeout delays), and B's 5/30/1 ms timing-based tests carry some flake risk. However B's suite covers more of the issue's variants table: 3 levels with slow middle, 4 levels with slow intermediates, plain div between levels, a sync middle, and provide/inject propagation at each level, plus the resolved-and-moved case. Both would fail on base.

Scope and craft are comparable; B's restructure is slightly larger but clearly commented and keeps the fix readable. Net: B resolves the root cause more completely with broader issue-aligned coverage, outweighing A's cleaner test style.

title: The Playground's TS version is set to 7 by default.

judge.reasoning: Both patches change the playground's default TypeScript version from 'latest' to a concrete 6.x release by passing `typescriptVersion: ref('6.0.3')` to `useStore`, and the independent tests confirm both fix the fresh-open and shared-link-without-version scenarios. The difference is in completeness and tests. Patch B is a one-line default change: a user can still pick a 7.x version from the dropdown and hit the same broken type support with no hint, and a shared link carrying 'latest' or 7.x still lands on a broken state. Patch A addresses the issue's actual complaint ('they don't know that Vue doesn't support TS7') by centralizing the policy in a small `typescript.ts` module: a `MAX_SUPPORTED_TS_MAJOR` constant with a comment explaining why, a `DEFAULT_TS_VERSION`, an `isSupportedTsVersion` guard, and `filterTsVersions` that removes 7+ from the VersionSelect list alongside the existing dev/insiders filter. It also resets an unsupported version coming from the URL hash, which is defensible since that state is unusable anyway. The extra scope is modest, directly tied to the issue's stated concern, and easy to revert when TS 7 is supported (bump one constant). Patch A adds a real unit test file exercising the default, the guard, and the list filter, which would fail on base (no module, and the old filter passes 7.x through); Patch B adds no tests. Craft-wise, Patch A's naming and comments are clear and consistent with the surrounding code, and the assignment to `store.typescriptVersion` works with the reactive store's ref unwrapping. Patch B is correct but minimal and untested, so A is the better fix.

+// TypeScript 7 (the native port) does not ship the JS API that the Vue
+// language tools in the REPL rely on, so type support breaks with it.
+// Default to (and only offer) versions below this major until it is supported.
+export const MAX_SUPPORTED_TS_MAJOR = 6
+
+// keep in sync with the latest supported TypeScript release
+export const DEFAULT_TS_VERSION = '6.0.3'
+
+export function isSupportedTsVersion(version: string): boolean {
+  if (version === 'latest') return false
+  const major = parseInt(version.replace(/^v/, ''), 10)
+  return !Number.isNaN(major) && major <= MAX_SUPPORTED_TS_MAJOR
+}
+
+export function filterTsVersions(versions: string[]): string[] {
+  return versions.filter(
+    v =>
+      !v.includes('dev') && !v.includes('insiders') && isSupportedTsVersion(v),
+  )
+}

title: KeepAlive caches a never-mounted vnode when a switch lands while an ancestor Suspense is pending

judge.reasoning: Both patches stop the crash by refusing to cache the never-mounted vnode, and the independent tests confirm both clear the reported errors. Patch B is exactly the issue's suggested one-line guard, but it leaves the rest of KeepAlive's bookkeeping inconsistent with what actually mounted: the render pass has already added the unmounted PageB's key to `keys` and set `current` to the unmounted vnode. With `max` set (the issue's real-world Nuxt `keepalive: { max: 5 }` case) that orphan key consumes a slot and causes an early prune of a live entry; pruneCacheEntry then finds no cached vnode and falls into the `resetShapeFlag(current)` branch against a vnode that was never mounted, and the still-active PageA branch can be evicted/unmounted out from under the inner Suspense. onBeforeUnmount likewise compares cache entries against the unmounted PageB child instead of the mounted PageA active branch, so PageA is unmounted via the cache loop while also being the Suspense's active branch. Patch A addresses these: getMountedInnerChild resolves to the Suspense branch that is actually mounted, setCache drops the orphan key, repoints `current`, and caches the mounted vnode under its own key (skipping if pruned), and onBeforeUnmount uses the mounted child. Its tests cover the plain switch, switch-then-unmount (asserting onUnmounted fires exactly once), and the `max` scenario (asserting PageA is neither evicted nor unmounted and PageC renders), which would fail on base and would expose B's max-eviction behavior. Patch A is more code and carries some complexity risk, but it is confined to the KeepAlive cache path and matches surrounding conventions (reuses keys/cache/current, comment style). Patch B's single test is adequate but narrower. On correctness under the issue's own scenarios, A is the better fix.

issue_md:
### Vue version

3.5.41 (also reproduces on 3.5.40 and 3.6.0-rc.3)

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://play.vuejs.org/#

### Steps to reproduce

The reproduction drives itself from `onMounted` — just open it and read the log. The tree is the one Nuxt renders for a page with `<NuxtPage keepalive>`:

```
<Suspense>            <!-- root boundary, still pending -->
  <RootDep />         <!-- async setup, resolves after 300ms -->
  <KeepAlive>
    <Suspense>        <!-- per-page boundary -->
      <component :is="page" :key="key" />
    </Suspense>
  </KeepAlive>
</Suspense>
```

1. While `RootDep` is still pending (so `parentSuspense.deps > 0`), switch the inner page from `PageA` to `PageB`.
2. Let the root boundary resolve.
3. Switch back to `PageA`, then to `PageB` again.

### What is expected?

The inner page follows the switches, and no errors are raised.

### What is actually happening?

The rendered page is stuck on `PageA` forever — every later switch is a no-op — and the renderer throws:

```
Cannot read properties of null (reading 'suspenseId')   // patchSuspense
Cannot read properties of null (reading 'm')            // unmountComponent
```

In a production build the second one is the more familiar
`Uncaught (in promise) TypeError: Cannot destructure property 'bum' of 'instance' as it is null.`

Removing the `<KeepAlive>` and changing nothing else makes both errors go away and navigation work.

### System Info

```shell
  System:
    OS: Linux 7.0 Ubuntu 26.04 LTS
    CPU: (4) x64 Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-8700 CPU @ 3.20GHz
    Memory: 5.86 GB / 11.67 GB
  Binaries:
    Node: 24.19.0
    npm: 11.19.0
  npmPackages:
    vue: 3.5.41
  Browsers:
    Chromium (Playwright 1.5x, headless)
```

### Any additional comments?

**The chain**, as far as I could trace it:

1. The route change re-renders `KeepAlive`, so the inner `<Suspense>` is patched with `n1 != null`. Because an **ancestor** boundary is still pending, `SuspenseImpl.process` takes its early return:

   ```js
   if (parentSuspense && parentSuspense.deps > 0 && !n1.suspense.isInFallback) {
     n2.suspense = n1.suspense
     n2.suspense.vnode = n2
     n2.el = n1.el
     return
   }
   ```

   The incoming page vnode is therefore never patched: `vnode.component === null`, `vnode.el === null`.

2. `KeepAlive`'s `onUpdated` → `cacheSubtree` still caches it, unconditionally:

   ```js
   if (isSuspense(instance.subTree.type)) {
     queuePostRenderEffect(() => {
       cache.set(pendingCacheKey, getInnerChild(instance.subTree))
     }, instance.subTree.suspense)
   }
   ```

3. The next render for that key hits the poisoned entry: `KeepAlive` copies `cachedVNode.component` (`null`) onto the new vnode and sets `COMPONENT_KEPT_ALIVE`, so `patchSuspense` reads `newBranch.component.suspenseId` on `null`, and the teardown that follows calls `unmountComponent(null)`.

**Suggested fix** — the same shape as the two guards already at that site, i.e. do not cache a vnode that never finished mounting:

```js
const innerChild = getInnerChild(instance.subTree)
if (innerChild.component) {
  cache.set(pendingCacheKey, innerChild)
}
```

With that guard the page is simply not cached that one time, and the reproduction runs clean.

This looks like a third path into the defect class fixed by #10912 (`avoid caching vnode that not been mounted`, for #10899) and #11479 (for #6028) — both guard `KeepAlive`'s **own** subtree, while here it is an **ancestor** `Suspense` that is pending.

Real-world context: this is how it surfaced for us — a Nuxt 4 app rendering `<NuxtPage :keepalive="{ max: 5 }" />`, where a link clicked before hydration finished intermittently left the user on a blank page with `Cannot destructure property 'bum' of 'e' as it is null` in the console. The window widens with slower hydration, so it shows up under load / on slow clients.

<sub>Investigation and reproduction prepared with Claude Code, on behalf of drunomics.</sub>

title: looseEqual() reports Map and Set instances with different contents as equal

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the root cause the same way: they add explicit `isMap`/`isSet` branches to `looseEqual` with order-insensitive, loosely-compared, one-to-one matching of entries, and both pass all eight independent tests that failed on base. Neither is a symptom mask. Correctness is effectively equal; both handle size mismatch, duplicate-looking members (via a used/matched array), Map-vs-Set, and Map-vs-plain-object. Patch B's implementation is simpler (one `looseCompareCollections` that reuses array comparison for `[key, value]` entries), which is a point in its favour, while Patch A's `looseCompareEntries` with three callbacks is heavier, though its identical-reference fast path is a sensible optimisation. Where they differ meaningfully is placement and tests. Patch A inserts the branches alongside the existing Date/Symbol/Array branches before the generic `isObject` check, exactly the pattern the issue suggests and the file already uses; Patch B nests them inside the object branch, which works but breaks the file's flat type-dispatch convention. Patch A's tests are substantially more thorough: empty maps/sets in both argument orders, key/order insensitivity, nested maps, loose object keys, the one-to-one matching rule, string-vs-collection mismatches, plus v-model tests covering select changes over time and radio/checkbox, which the issue cites as the user-facing symptom. Patch B's tests cover the core cases but are thinner and its v-model test checks only initial selection. On balance A edges out B on tests and convention consistency, with correctness tied and B's simpler helper not enough to offset that.

issue_md:
### Vue version

3.5.x / `main` (verified at `a2b40db`)

### Link to minimal reproduction

Reproducible directly against the repo (see below) — `looseEqual` is not exported publicly, so the SFC Playground can only show the `v-model` symptom, not the root cause.

### Steps to reproduce

`looseEqual()` in `packages/shared/src/looseEqual.ts` reports unrelated `Map` and `Set` instances as equal:

```ts
import { looseEqual } from '@vue/shared'

looseEqual(new Map([['a', 1]]), new Map([['b', 2]])) // true, expected false
looseEqual(new Set([1]), new Set([2]))               // true, expected false
looseEqual(new Map([['a', 1]]), new Map())           // true, expected false
```

This surfaces to users through `v-model` on `<select>`. The following selects the **wrong** option:

```ts
const mapA = new Map([['id', 1]])
const mapB = new Map([['id', 2]])
const selected = ref(mapB)
```

```vue
<select v-model="selected">
  <option :value="mapA">A</option>
  <option :value="mapB">B</option>
</select>
```

`el.selectedIndex` is `0` (option A) when it should be `1`, because `looseEqual(mapA, mapB)` returns `true` and the loop in `setSelected` stops at the first option.

### What is expected?

`Map`/`Set` values with different contents compare as not equal, so `v-model` selects the option that actually matches.

### What is actually happening?

`Map` and `Set` fall through to the generic object branch. `Object.keys()` on either is always `[]`, so the key-count check passes and the `for...in` loop body never executes — entries are never compared. Execution then reaches the final line:

```ts
return String(a) === String(b)
```

Every `Map` stringifies to `'[object Map]'` and every `Set` to `'[object Set]'`, so any two of the same type are reported equal.

Note this differs from `Date` and `Symbol`, which are given explicit branches above, and from arrays and plain objects, which compare correctly:

```ts
looseEqual([1], [2])       // false, correct
looseEqual({ a: 1 }, { a: 2 }) // false, correct
```

`packages/shared/__tests__/looseEqual.spec.ts` has 13 cases but none for `Map`/`Set`, which is why this hasn't been caught.

### Possible fix

Add explicit branches before the generic object check, mirroring the existing `Date`/`Symbol` pattern. `isMap` and `isSet` already exist in `packages/shared/src/general.ts`. `Set` needs content comparison rather than reference lookup to stay consistent with `looseEqual`'s semantics (e.g. `new Set([{ a: 1 }])` vs `new Set([{ a: 1 }])`).

Worth confirming the intended semantics first: should `Map` comparison be key-order-insensitive, and should `Set` compare loosely (`looseEqual` per element) or strictly? Happy to open a PR with tests once the direction is confirmed.

### System Info

```
Vue: 3.5.x / main @ a2b40db
```

### Any additional comments?

Unrelated to #15298, which touches only `vModel.ts`.
